cells.tense: You're tending it now, and it's steady in your hands.
cells.verb: Tending what grows with a care that carries its own form
cells.place: Where something living is being brought along
cells.ask: Let someone see the care — offer one person a plain account of what you've been holding and keeping alive — and notice how finishing with something can feel like arriving, not losing it.
cells.core:
You're tending something that's alive, and you're doing it with both hands. Not forcing it toward a shape it doesn't have, not letting it run wild either — you've found the pace it actually grows at, and you're keeping to it. The work mostly looks like attention: you notice what's changing, you adjust, and you don't panic when nothing moves for a while. That steadiness is what lets the thing in front of you become what it is.

What you're carrying rarely makes it into words. Someone sees the result and calls it lucky, or takes it for granted, and you let that stand — but the days of tending are the part that was actually you. Naming them isn't boasting. It's letting the care be visible where it's been invisible, and it takes less out of you than keeping it hidden. When the thing is finished, you'll be free to let it go. Finishing is how you get there — not a failure, just the far edge of having cared well.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending something alive, and you're letting it grow at its own pace.

cells.tense: You're moving toward a version of it that isn't here yet.
cells.verb: Steering a living thing toward the shape you've already decided it should take
cells.place: Where growth is happening, though on a timetable you want sooner
cells.ask: Let one thing you're tending develop without a hand on it for a while — and give yourself over to a stretch of unforced imagining, the kind that only comes once what you've lived through has been allowed to settle.
cells.core:
You're not tending it anymore — you're steering it. There's a version of this that's finished, healthy, whole, and you're already living out of that version and pulling hard to make it real. Every check, every correction, every quiet read of how it's doing — it's all working toward a picture that hasn't happened yet. You're pushing a living thing on a schedule it didn't agree to.

From the outside it looks like care, and some of it is. But you've noticed that it exhausts you in a way tending never did. The grip is the tell. Vision doesn't come from keeping a thing clamped in place; it comes from having lived enough that the imagining has somewhere to rise from. If you let one part of this happen at its own speed, you'll find out what it actually becomes — and what you actually want. Reaching that is not giving up. It's arriving.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering a living thing instead of letting it grow.

cells.tense: You meant to step back toward it, and you haven't.
cells.verb: Withholding your hand from something that still needs tending
cells.place: Where what's growing is doing it without your attention
cells.ask: Give your persistence one thing to keep reaching toward — a hope you're still willing to hold out loud — and let what you've grown so far be seen shining in its own right before you decide it means nothing.
cells.core:
There's something growing here that you've pulled your hands away from. Not because you stopped caring — but because care turned expensive, and staying at a distance is easier than being present and watching it not work the way you hoped. You can still name it, can still tell me exactly what it needs. You just aren't the one doing it anymore, and you've been calling that distance wisdom when it's really just distance.

What's still here is stubborn — endurance, wanting to keep hoping even when nothing's confirmed. You can point that at something, even one small thing, and your hands will come back to it. The other half of this: let something you've already brought along be seen for what it is. Radiance doesn't come from a new start. It comes from what you cultivated reaching the end of its growing. Look at that before you write it off.
cells.sheetLine: You pulled your hands away from something still growing.

lint.detail: the tense sentence does not read as Too Little's time

cells.tense: You're already tending it — the hands are moving on their own.
cells.verb: Keeping something alive with care you don't count as care
cells.place: Where growth is happening because of what you do daily
cells.ask: Say out loud one thing you're tending that you've been calling just how things work — and let it be known that it costs you something.
cells.core:
Something's growing here — you water it, you check on it, you keep it going through weeks that don't show in any ledger. Ask you about it and you'll shrug, say it's just what needs doing, that anyone would. The tending is running; your name isn't on it.

That's the whole gap: what you do with your hands every day is stewardship, and what you tell the world — including yourself — is that it's maintenance. Whoever gets the benefit rarely knows it came from you, because you've arranged it that way. Naming one of those acts as care doesn't cost you anything. It isn't a request for thanks. It's just leaving the receipt where it belongs — and letting the thing end, when its time comes, without shame.
cells.sheetLine: You tend something every day and call it nothing.
